name: Bonomarlot

b.x: Bonomarlot (also designated A-20, CAS number not publicly assigned) is a Cytomax class bioregulator produced from the bone marrow of young calves, designed to support hematopoietic function. The theoretical basis comes from replicated Khavinson laboratory studies [1] [2] showing that short peptides can enter cell nuclei and alter gene expression. It contains a mixture of short-chain peptides, typically 2 to 7 amino acids long, extracted and standardized at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology. The product ships as oral capsules containing 10 mg of peptide complex each. Bone marrow is where hematopoiesis happens. Red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets; they all originate from hematopoietic stem cells housed in that tissue. Age-related decline in marrow function contributes to immunosenescence, subclinical anemia, and reduced regenerative capacity. Bonomarlot's proposed job is to restore gene expression patterns in aging bone marrow cells by supplying tissue-specific peptide fragments that interact with DNA promoter regions. The honest assessment: zero Bonomarlot-specific clinical trials appear in PubMed. Community use is niche, with fewer than 50 indexed reports across English-language forums. Users follow manufacturer protocols closely and track results through CBC bloodwork rather than subjective effects. Pricing runs $135 to $190 per 60-capsule box.

The Khavinson bioregulator model proposes a specific chain of events. Small peptides survive gastric digestion because of their size. They cross the intestinal wall through PepT1 (SLC15A1) and LAT family transporters. Once in systemic circulation, they distribute to bone marrow tissue and enter target cells. Inside the nucleus, these peptides interact with nucleosomes and histone proteins at specific DNA sequences. Khavinson et al. [1] tested the related peptides AED, KED, and KE in human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. IGF1 expression increased 3.5 to 5.6-fold. FOXO1 and TERT gene activity also changed, both linked to cellular senescence pathways. A separate line of research supports bone marrow peptide signaling from a different angle. Petrov and Mikhailova identified endogenous regulatory hexapeptides (MP-1 and MP-2) produced by bone marrow cells themselves [3] [4]. MP-1 stimulated antibody production up to 2.5-fold. MP-2 reversed tumor-induced T-lymphocyte suppression. These myelopeptides share structural homology with hemoglobin chain fragments, pointing to a conserved signaling function. Bonomarlot is theorized to supplement declining endogenous peptide signaling in aging marrow. Direct evidence for this product's intracellular activity has not been published.
Bonomarlot benefits center on bone marrow support and hematopoietic maintenance in aging adults.
Targets bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells through tissue-specific peptide fragments, following the Khavinson organ-specificity model validated in MSC culture [1].
Oral capsule format. No reconstitution, no injection, no cold chain during use. Two capsules daily with water before a meal.

Related Khavinson peptides boosted IGF1 expression 3.5 to 5.6-fold and modulated FOXO1 and TERT in human bone marrow stem cells; Bonomarlot aims to reproduce this gene expression effect via the oral route.
Community users report improved immune resilience over months following a course, with fewer illness episodes tracked across repeat cycles.
Designed for pulsed cycling (10 to 30 days on, months off), meaning annual cost stays between $270 and $380 for a standard maintenance protocol.
Stacks with Thymalin (thymus), Epithalon (pineal), and Crystagen (thymic tripeptide) in the classic Khavinson immune-longevity framework.

Supporting evidence is class-level only: Khavinson et al. 2020 [1] demonstrated gene expression modulation by AED/KED/KE short peptides in human bone marrow MSCs. Myelopeptide research (Petrov et al.) [3] [4] establishes that bone-marrow-derived hexapeptides have immunoregulatory activity. Direct hematopoietic benefit from oral Bonomarlot is undemonstrated in published controlled trials.

Khavinson et al. 2020 (PMID 32399807): gene expression modulation by short peptides in human bone marrow MSCs (class evidence; not Bonomarlot-specific)
Limitations

Zero Bonomarlot-specific RCTs or PubMed-indexed clinical trials; all supporting data is extrapolated from related Khavinson peptides (AED/KED/KE) or myelopeptide pharmacology; oral short-peptide bioavailability estimated 10–30% with no Bonomarlot PK study; Russian-language clinical documentation not indexed in English databases

Community protocols mirror manufacturer (Khavinson Institute / Firma-Vita) dosing exactly. The underlying class-level science supports the short-peptide gene expression mechanism. Alignment exists on cycling rationale and dose range; divergence exists on evidence quality: the community operates on the broader Khavinson framework while Bonomarlot-specific trial data is absent.
Community Khavinson Institute protocol

Bonomarlot is an oral capsule product. No reconstitution, no bacteriostatic water, no syringes. Each capsule contains 10 mg of peptide complex. The standard protocol is straightforward: 2 capsules daily, 15 to 20 minutes before a meal, with a small amount of water. Swallow them whole. Don't chew or open the capsules. For a first-time user, the recommendation is a 30-day loading course before switching to 10-day maintenance courses every 3 to 6 months. If your CBC is normal and you're doing this preventively, the 10-day course twice yearly is sufficient. The thing most beginners miss: you won't feel anything. Bonomarlot produces no subjective effects. Get a CBC before your first course and again 4 weeks after finishing. Without baseline labs, you have no way to assess whether it's working. Ferritin, B12, and folate at baseline help rule out nutritional causes of low blood counts so you don't attribute improvements to a peptide when iron was the issue. Store capsules at room temperature (15 to 25 degrees Celsius). Keep them dry and out of direct sunlight. No refrigeration needed for sealed blister packs.
Cycling Protocol

Standard Khavinson bioregulator protocol is 10-30 days on, then repeat every 3-6 months. A typical maintenance cycle is 2 capsules daily for 10 days, repeated twice per year. Therapeutic protocols may extend to 30 days. This cycling approach comes from the general Khavinson bioregulator framework: no Bonomarlot-specific cycling studies have been published. Some practitioners combine Bonomarlot with other bioregulators (Thymalin, Crystagen, Vladonix) in staggered cycles targeting different aspects of immune function.
Bonomarlot Cycle

Cycling in the Khavinson model is not driven by receptor desensitization or hormonal axis suppression. The proposed mechanism is epigenetic: short peptides modulate gene expression in bone marrow cells, and these expression changes persist for 3–6 months after the peptide is cleared. Continuous daily dosing adds no benefit once gene expression normalization is achieved: excess peptides are catabolized as amino acids. Cycling is intrinsic to the mechanism of action, not a safety precaution.
Effects do not intensify with continuous daily use: plateau is expected
CBC trends (when positive) persist 3–6 months post-course, consistent with the residual epigenetic effect model
Related Khavinson peptides (AED/KED) show persistent IGF1/FOXO1 expression changes beyond active dosing in MSC culture studies

Avoid
Chemotherapy agents (any myelosuppressive)

Bone marrow-targeting peptides may interact unpredictably with myelosuppressive chemotherapy. No safety or interaction data exists; concurrent use poses undefined risk of altering myelosuppression depth or recovery kinetics.
Immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus)
Bonomarlot theoretically stimulates bone marrow immune output; counteracting immunosuppression in transplant recipients could precipitate rejection. Explicit contraindication.
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (EPO, darbepoetin)
Additive bone marrow stimulation is theoretically possible; no interaction data or safety monitoring guidance exists.
G-CSF / GM-CSF (filgrastim, sargramostim)
Concurrent bone marrow stimulation with hematopoietic growth factors is unstudied; potential for excessive or dysregulated hematopoietic activation.

The most serious consideration with Bonomarlot is what it might do in people who should not take it, not what it does in healthy users. Active hematologic malignancies (leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma) are an explicit contraindication. Stimulating bone marrow activity in the presence of malignant hematopoietic cells could accelerate disease progression; no safety data exists for this scenario. Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy face a related concern. Bonomarlot theoretically stimulates bone marrow immune output. Counteracting immunosuppression with cyclosporine or tacrolimus could precipitate graft rejection. This interaction is theoretical but the stakes make it a hard avoid. For healthy adults following standard protocols, the side effect profile appears mild based on limited user reports. Occasional gastrointestinal discomfort (nausea, bloating) is possible with any oral peptide product. These symptoms, when reported, typically resolve by day 2 or 3 of a course. Allergic reactions are theoretically possible. Bonomarlot is extracted from bovine bone marrow tissue. Anyone with a known allergy to bovine-derived products should not use it. Excipient composition varies by product: one formulation contains lactose and Tween-80, while another uses carrageenan and HPMC. Users with excipient sensitivities should check the ingredient list on the label. The human safety dataset is effectively zero for Bonomarlot specifically. No controlled tolerability study has been published in indexed literature. Most safety inferences come from the broader Khavinson bioregulator program, where adverse event rates across multiple products have been low in Russian-language clinical documentation. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are contraindicated. No reproductive safety data exists. Children under 18 should not use this product; no pediatric dosing or safety information is available. Concurrent use with chemotherapy agents poses undefined risk. Bone marrow-targeting peptides could alter myelosuppression depth or recovery kinetics in unpredictable ways. EPO, darbepoetin, filgrastim, and sargramostim carry similar theoretical interaction concerns due to additive bone marrow stimulation. Stop use and consult a physician if you develop urticaria, persistent GI distress, or worsening CBC trends on repeat testing.
Common Issues & Solutions

No perceived effect without labs: Bonomarlot produces no subjective symptoms; CBC before and after each course is the only objective efficacy proxy. Expecting a felt response without tracking bloodwork sets up false negative conclusions.

Skipping the 30-day loading course: Starting with 10-day maintenance alone may underdeliver, particularly in documented deficiency states; Khavinson protocols specify the intensive loading course first.

Repeating courses too frequently: The proposed 3–6 month residual effect means courses taken more often than every 2 months produce overlap, not compounding; excess doses are metabolized as amino acids without additional benefit.

Treating as a cancer therapy: Some product listings name "complex oncology treatment" as an indication; this is unsupported by any accessible clinical trial. Active malignancy is a contraindication, not an indication for self-directed use.
Secondary-market product: budget listings (~$85) and marketplace listings offer no cold-chain or provenance assurance.

Bonomarlot is classified as a dietary supplement in Russia and several CIS countries, where it is manufactured by Firma-Vita under the Khavinson Institute licensee framework. It is not FDA-approved or regulated as a drug in the United States. In the U.S., Bonomarlot is not on FDA's compounding lists. It appears in no 503A or 503B category (May 14, 2026; March 21, 2025) and not in 21 CFR 216.23. It is imported as a dietary supplement or for personal use. No DEA scheduling applies. WADA's 2026 Prohibited List does not name Bonomarlot. The product has no assigned CAS number in Western chemical databases. No NDA, IND, or formal regulatory application has been filed with any Western drug agency. This content is for educational and informational purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice. Consult a qualified healthcare provider before starting any peptide protocol. Peptide Schedule does not sell or endorse any peptide product.

faqs.q: Do I need to cycle Bonomarlot or can I take it continuously?
faqs.a: Bonomarlot is designed for pulsed cycling, not continuous use. The standard protocol is a 30-day intensive loading course, then 10-day maintenance courses every 2–3 months. Effects accumulate and persist for 3–6 months after a course ends; continuous daily use adds no advantage and is not manufacturer-recommended.

faqs.q: Will Bonomarlot show up on bloodwork and how do I know if it's working?
faqs.a: No commercial assay exists for the A-20 peptide complex. The practical approach is CBC before and after a 30-day course. RBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit, WBC differential, platelet count. Meaningful improvements in these markers would be the expected signal. Baseline labs are essential; without them, efficacy assessment is impossible.

faqs.q: Can I stack Bonomarlot with other Khavinson bioregulators?
faqs.a: Stacking is common in the longevity community. Common combinations include Thymalin (thymus) + Epithalon (pineal) as a foundation immune-longevity stack. No pharmacokinetic interaction data exists; the assumption is organ-specific bioregulators act independently at the cellular level.

faqs.q: Is Bonomarlot safe for post-chemotherapy bone marrow recovery?
faqs.a: Product documentation lists post-chemotherapy bone marrow support as an intended indication. However, no clinical trial validates concurrent use with active chemotherapy, and no oncologist-reviewed safety data exists in indexed English literature. Active hematologic malignancies are an explicit contraindication. Anyone in active cancer treatment should get oncologist clearance first.

faqs.q: Is there a meaningful difference between Cytomax Bonomarlot and synthetic bone marrow peptides?
faqs.a: Bonomarlot is a Cytomax, a multi-peptide complex extracted from young calf bone marrow containing 2–7 AA peptides. Commercial product literature holds that Cytomaxes have longer downstream effects due to multi-peptide complexity, while Cytogens act faster with shorter duration. No comparative RCT exists to validate this.

faqs.q: What is the recommended Bonomarlot dosage?
faqs.a: Bonomarlot dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 10 mg daily, moderate users at 20 mg daily, and aggressive protocols use 20 mg 2x daily.

faqs.q: Does Bonomarlot need to be reconstituted?
faqs.a: No. Bonomarlot is taken by mouth and is not reconstituted with bacteriostatic water.
